sources.title: German Archaeological Institute, investigations at the Great Dam of Marib

sources.basis: Archaeological discussion places final destruction sometime 570–600; exodus and genealogical destinations remain traditional accounts.

estimates.name: Arab homeland · Qarqar-era context
estimates.basis: The 853 BCE inscription records Gindibu’s Arab contingent at Qarqar, not the location or size of all Arabs. Northwest Arabia and Jordan are the user’s reconstructed starting homeland. People begin in place; no migration to Qarqar is asserted. Two regional components of 10,000 households each ×5 people =100,000 central people; this is a declared reference-class prior, not a count inferred from Qarqar’s 1,000 camels. Low/high are sensitivity scenarios, not confidence intervals.

estimates.name: Arab groups · interior Syrian and Iraqi deserts
estimates.basis: Tiglath-pileser III received Zabibe’s tribute in 738 BCE;745 is his accession year. Samsi’s defeat belongs to 733–732 BCE. Slow inland northward spread is reconstructed from the user’s reasoning, avoiding the Levantine coast; tribute is not itself a documented migration. The central 20,000 people are an explicitly allocated subset of the 100,000-person homeland; no new copy is added. Low/high are sensitivity scenarios, not confidence intervals.

estimates.name: Lakhmid-associated Arab presence at Hira
estimates.basis: The Lakhmid house emerged in the late third century, with a kingdom conventionally dated around 300–602. The 328 Namara inscription is a later attestation, not a founding date. This is an associated regional population reconstruction, not a population map derived from state borders. The major-regional-settlement reference class uses 4,000 households ×5 people =20,000 central people; no population is inferred from royal territory. Low/high are sensitivity scenarios, not confidence intervals.

milestones.title: Arab homeland · 853 BCE
milestones.text: Arab communities are already present in northwest Arabia and Jordan.

milestones.title: Tribute-era inland spread
milestones.text: Zabibe’s 738 BCE tribute; slow northward movement into the Syrian and Iraqi deserts.

milestones.title: Slow spread through Arabia
milestones.text: South through the Hijaz toward Yemen and Marib, with a smaller inland branch toward the Gulf and Oman.

milestones.title: Arabs in interior Syria
milestones.text: Emesa and Hawran communities appear as regional presences around the turn of the era.

milestones.title: Tanukh and the late-antique client world
milestones.text: Tanukh moves toward the lower Euphrates and Hira.

milestones.title: Elagabalus · 218–222 CE
milestones.text: The Emesene dynasty and Arab communities of interior Syria.

milestones.title: Philip the Arab · 244–249 CE
milestones.text: Philip’s reign and the communities around Shahba.

milestones.title: Lakhmids at Hira
milestones.text: Late-third-century establishment; dynasty approximately 300–602 CE. Tanukh remains a distinct source cohort.

milestones.title: Ghassan and the Syrian frontier
milestones.text: Ghassan settlement has earlier traditions; the Jafnid Byzantine federation belongs especially to the sixth century.

milestones.title: Ghassanid federation · Hawran and Golan
milestones.text: The Byzantine frontier federation in Hawran and Golan.

milestones.title: Marib · documented repair
milestones.text: Abraha’s 548 CE repair precedes the traditional final-collapse and exodus accounts.

milestones.title: Marib departures
milestones.text: People leave Marib for northern and western destinations.

milestones.title: Register migrations continue
milestones.text: The supplied register continues alongside the accumulated earlier populations.

populationAccounting: Initial 100,000 household-equivalent people. The standing-ledger layer supplies all subsequent groups by transfers and one declared natural-growth model; early labels do not create additional cohorts.
